The epistemology operates on six primitives: claim, warrant, status, gap, conflict, and ruling.
Claim is an assertion that something is the case.
Claim is the atomic unit of Chirality's epistemology.
Every non-trivial assertion produced by an agent in a governed workflow is a claim.
Warrant is the justification for believing a claim.
Warrant is always extrinsic.
A warrant is a source citation using file, section, and quote.
Model confidence is not a warrant.
Plausibility is not a warrant.
Status is the epistemic classification of a claim's certainty.
Status is expressed as FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, or TBD.
Gap is an explicit positive assertion that a warrant has not been found.
Gap represents absence of information as a visible and actionable entity.
Conflict is two or more claims with incompatible warrants about the same key.
Conflict must be resolved before the deliverable can advance.
Ruling is a human decision that resolves a gap or conflict.
Rulings transform epistemic status.
Rulings are binding and recorded in versioned files.
K-PROV-1 governs warrants by requiring every claim to have an extrinsic warrant or explicit location TBD.
K-INVENT-1 governs gaps by requiring missing data to be represented rather than fabricated.
K-CONFLICT-1 governs conflicts by requiring disagreements to be exposed rather than silently resolved.
K-AUTH-1 governs rulings by reserving binding rulings and approval records for humans.
K-AUTH-2 makes the warrant-to-content binding mechanically verifiable.
A claim has a status.
A claim may have a warrant.
A claim without a warrant has status TBD or ASSUMPTION.
Two claims may be in conflict.
A conflict requires a ruling.
A ruling transforms claim status.

Chirality treats the pairing of knowledge components as constitutive.

Several traditions articulate knowledge as irreducible complementary components without using the chirality metaphor.
Bohr's complementarity is the closest formal precedent for chirality.
Bohr's complementarity describes two descriptions both required to explain a phenomenon.
Bohr's complementary descriptions are mutually irreducible.
Bohr's complementary descriptions resist synthesis into a unified account.
Bohr extended complementarity beyond physics to epistemology, psychology, and biology.
Plotnitsky developed complementarity into a general epistemological principle.
Plotnitsky treats each side of a subject-object relation as requiring a separate mode of description.

Claim and warrant are not alternative descriptions that exclude each other.

Polanyi describes knowing as a from-to polar structure.

Polanyi insists that all knowing involves personal commitment.

Polanyi and Prosch extend the from-to structure into a theory of meaning as an achievement of committed persons.
Sellars' space of reasons supports irreducibility of the two knowledge components.
Sellars distinguishes the logical space of reasons from causal or empirical description.
McDowell later formalized the contrast as space of reasons versus realm of law.
Epistemic facts cannot be fully analyzed into non-epistemic facts.
The causal order and justificatory order are structurally different.
Neither causal order nor justificatory order can be reduced to the other.
Knowledge requires both causal connection to the world and placement in the space of reasons.
AI agents operate in the space of causes by producing outputs through next-token prediction.
Knowledge lives in the space of reasons where claims are warranted and accepted by accountable persons.
Chirality's epistemic architecture bridges the space of causes and the space of reasons.
